title: Dhūnī-tap – Wherever There is Fire There is The Name
creator: Prema Goet
description: The moving-picture work “Dhūnī-tap - Wherever There is Fire There is The Name” was filmed in Allahabad and Mathura, India, between January 2025 and March 2026. The work explores aspects of the visual culture surrounding the materiality of the ascetic practice of dhūnī tap, from which it derives its title. Structured in two parts, the film first attends to the material and performative dimensions of the saṃkalpa ritual before turning to the practice of dhūnī tap as undertaken by members of the Rāmānandī community. The film was deliberately shot on a 1971 Beaulieu 4008 ZM II moving-picture camera using Kodak Ektachrome 100 dia-positive colour film stock. This technical and aesthetic choice positions the work in formal contrast to the 35mm black-and-white photographic material presented throughout the Dhun-Dhūnī: The Fires of the Name exhibition. The film’s chromatic progression –  moving from faded and underexposed imagery toward increasingly saturated colour –  may be read as a visual counterpart to the conceptual and affective concerns articulated within the exhibition’s “Dhun” section. The soundtrack consists of a composite arrangement of field recordings produced between 2015 and 2026. Bringing together five discrete sonic segments, the composition seeks to evoke aspects of the auditory environments associated with spaces inhabited by the Rāmānandī community. In this respect, the work attempts to approximate the immersive acoustic conditions characteristic of such settings. Three of the five sonic segments are made available as part of the exhibition and are accessible on this website as individual audio files. One segment –  the synth component –  constitutes a deliberate compositional intervention introduced by the artist and does not derive from documentary field-recorded material.

title: Jagadīśa Dāsa Mahātyāgī, showing the sūrya mudrā
creator: Prema Goet
description: In this sequence of images, sādhu (holy man) Jagadīśa Dāsa Mahātyāgī of the Rāmānandī Sampradāya, a Vaishnava religious order, can be seen performing various mudrās during the dhūnī tap. Here, he demonstrates Sūrya-mudrā hand-gesture. This photograph was taken by Prema Goet during the Kumbha Mela in Ujjain, India, in 2015/2016, and printed at Fotoleutner in Vienna in 2026. It was acquired by Task Force 3 of the MANTRAMS project as part of Goet’s doctoral research at the University of Vienna. Between 2025 and 2028, the photograph was exhibited within the exhibition “Dhun / Dhūnī.The Fires of the Name,” presented during the Yoga Darśana Conference “Yoga Darśana, Yoga Sādhana: Authenticity, Authority, and Adaptation” in Paris, as well as in an exhibition at the Department of South Asian, Buddhist and Tibetan Studies at the University of Vienna in 2026.

title: Gaurimangal
creator: Prema Goet
description: Gauri Mangal, evening āratī, sung by a group of Rāmānandī tyāgis. Recorded at the Kumbha mela in Ujjain – 2016. Lead singers: Śastriji Mahārāj and Śri Rāmadasjī , drums by Ānanda Dāsa. Recorded Ujjain in 2016 by Prema Goet, who adds: “I recorded the Gaurī Maṅgal ārati at the invitation of, and with permission from, Śāstrījī Mahārāj, who is the main voice heard in this recording. The recording took place during the 2016 Ujjain Kumbha Melā. At that time, Vināyak Dāsa Tyāgī — who appears as the main character in the second part of the Dhūnī film —  was camping just outside the main tent where Śāstrījī Mahārāj and the others were staying. Mahārāj had invited me to the evening ārati several times before I finally attended it. One day, upon seeing me in the streets, he again asked whether I would come that evening. I arrived late at night and was only able to participate in the final half hour of it, but I was astonished by the strength and resilience of his singing. I knew I had to return the next day to experience the entire ārati from the beginning. The following evening I arrived on time, that is, before the ārati had begun. I asked Bābājī if I could record it, and he graciously agreed. At the end of this audio file, one can hear my voice saying, “It is still recording,” as Bābājī asked me to play the recording back to him. For the next ten minutes, Bābājī and the others listened very carefully to the playback from my Zoom H2n recorder. The recording contains selected verses from Rāmcaritmānas, Tulsidas’s rendering of the Rāmāyaṇa. This recitation moves among groups of ascetics and devotees, carried through song, call and response, and the melodic cycles of bhajan and kīrtan that structure the communal life of the Rāmānandī Sampradāya. These musical forms extend the Divine Name outward – into gatherings, processions, and shared ritual time. Here the lead singer –  Śāstrījī Mahārāj – chants selected verses in praise of Lord Rāma, while the surrounding assembly of ascetics responds with corresponding passages from the Epic. The chosen verses do not necessarily form a coherent sequence on their own, nor do they follow the narrative progression of the Rāmāyaṇa.”

title: SītāRām
creator: Prema Goet
description: This 30-minute audio recording was made at the Kumbha Melā in Ujjain, India, in April 2016. The musicians were followers of Śītārām Mahārāj, a prominent leader of the Mahātyāgī sect. Two of his disciples — Jagadīśa Dāsa Mahātyāgī and Gopāl Dāsa Mahātyāgī — are featured in the Dhun-Dhunī exhibition. At this camp, different groups of musicians would take turns performing continuously so that devotional music was maintained throughout all 24 hours of the day and night. The ensemble heard in this recording consisted primarily of devotees from Rajasthan.

title: Rām-Nām Montage Saturation
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: Rapid sequences of saturation and movement unfold through the city — walls, shrines, posters, vehicles, bustling markets, fading inscriptions, loudspeakers  chants, riverfront steps, and dense moving crowds — all layered with the living soundscape of an Indian town, where devotion, noise, and daily life merge into continuous flow. The images were captured with the intention of foto documenting the material manifestations of a sacred concept (Rām-Nām) in one of India's most popular pilgramage destinations. Specifically the capturing of the occurance of the name in specific contexts and frameworks was intended. Our intention was to highlight the pervasiveness of the sacred name in the socio-cultural physical landscape of the town.
subject: dhun; digital essay

title: The duality of Rām's name and His Saguṇa form
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: This video features the profound reflections of Narsingh Pandey on the divine mystery of Rām’s Name (Nām) and His Saguṇa form — the personal, visible manifestation of the Divine. Drawing from the teachings of the Rāmcaritamānas, the discourse explains how the two syllables “Rā” and “Ma” are themselves sweet, beautiful, and spiritually transformative. The gentleman on the ghat sells hand painted items with Rām-Nām. A conversation was struck with him on his personal reflections of the impact of ram nam on his life. The lady captured clapping her hands during was seen at an energetic arti ritual at a popular public temple in town. The women in the last frame were engaged in singing devotional songs to the accompaniment of instruments on an auspicious day.
subject: dhun; digital essay

title: Śiv and the glory of Rām-Nām
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: This video explores the spiritual glory of Rām-Nām as described in the Rāmcaritamānas, emphasizing the compassionate and liberating power of the divine name of Śrī Rām. The discourse highlights that even Śiv, together with  Pārvatī, constantly chants Rām-Nām, revealing its supreme significance in the Bhakti tradition. Through the dialogue between Pārvatī and Śiv, the video reflects on the spiritual struggles of humanity in Kali Yug and presents Rām-Nām as a simple yet powerful path accessible to all. It further explains that Śiv’s own strength — including His ability to consume the deadly Hālāhal poison — is rooted in the constant remembrance of Rām’s name. The video ultimately presents Rām-Nām as a source of protection, inner peace, purification, and liberation for all beings. The rearchers were seeking for expertise on contextual information regarding some content information of the project. During this quest they encountered a person sitting in public reciting some verses. Pandit Pandey was encrossed in reading verses from the Rāmcaritamāns before the south facing shrine of Hanuman. His chanting and the accompanying discourse gave evidence to the observers that he displayed prolific knowledge of the text.
subject: dhun; digital essay

title: The power of writing Rām-Nām
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: An edited interview with the manager of the Ram Ramapati Bank talking about his family, personal and bussiness relationship with the practice.
subject: dhun; digital essay

title: Kabīr’s vision of Rām
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: Umesh Kabir Ji of the Kabīr Caurā Maṭh, Varanasi explains the deeper meaning of Kabīr’s teachings on the remembrance of Rām. This vision transcends physicality and looks at Rām as being much beyond the hero of the epic tradition. Kabīr’s Rām is meant to be the object of deep contemplation and constant remembrance. In that sense He is accessible as a means of spiritual upliftment for all, irrespective of the social boundaries which may divide them.
subject: dhun; digital essay

title: Jap in the air
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: Suspended between continents and time zones, a woman practices jap (जप, jap — the repetitive chanting of a mantra for meditation and spiritual focus) while flying through the night. In one hand, an electronic jap counter quietly tracks each mantra; in the other, an endless Instagram feed glows against the dim airplane cabin.
subject: dhun; digital essay

title: How Śiv bestows Mokṣ in Kāśī
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: This video explores the sacred connection between Kāśī, Śiv, and the liberating power of Rām-Nām as described in the Rāmcaritamānas. The discourse explains that Śiv — the embodiment of wisdom — constantly chants the name of Śrī Rām, affirming the supreme glory of Rām-Nām above all other mantras. The video centers on the traditional belief that liberation (Mokṣ) is attained in Kāśī through the grace of Śiv and the power of the Rām Tārak Mantra. It explains that when beings leave their bodies in Kāśī, Śiv Himself grants liberation by whispering the divine name of Rām into their ears. Even the smallest creatures are said to receive this grace, emphasizing the boundless compassion associated with Kāśī and the divine name. Through these teachings, the video presents Kāśī not merely as a physical city, but as a spiritual realm of grace, where devotion to Śrī Rāmcandra and the chanting of his divine name become the pathway to liberation. The rearchers were seeking for expertise on contextual information  regarding some content information of the project. During this quest they encountered a person sitting in public reciting some verses. Pandit Pandey was encrossed in reading verses from the Rāmcaritamānas before the south facing shrine of Hanuman. His chanting and the accompanying discourse gave evidence to the observers that he displayed prolific knowledge of the text. The two overlay images resonate with the themes spoken of by Pandit Pandey in the interview. The first imag shows Rām-Nām in Devanagari written over a Śiv lingam. The Tarakeshwar Temple enshrines Siv in his aspect as the one who whispers the Tārak Mantra into the ears of a dying person.
subject: dhun; digital essay

title: Clay Pot on the Sands of Ganges
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: A solitary clay pot rests on the sunlit sands of the Ganges, while the solemn chant “Rām Nām Saty Hai” echoes. It whispers of life’s fleeting moments, the return of all to the river, and the eternal dance of death, rebirth, and the sacred flow that carries souls beyond the mortal shore.
subject: dhun; digital essay

title: Encountering the name and saturation (DHUN Gallery 1)
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: The name “Rām” surfaces on plastic keychains beside packets of incense, handwritten into notebooks, traced repeatedly with fingers across metal grills designed to form the sacred name, smeared on trees, sprayed on walls, carved into prayer beads, printed on cloth, on commercial stalls, temples, streets, shrines, markets, and objects. The symbol circulates around different surfaces, spaces and contexts. It is seen, heard and touched. There is rarely any space where the name can not be encountered as illustrated by the images.

title: Mobilising the name / Ram of Ram raj (DHUN Gallery 2)
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: The name becomes spatial. Across the city, chants, symbols, and visual signs associated with politics appear on mass produced bazaar paraphenalia, flags, fabrics, garments, and digital surfaces. Repeated across streets, walls, bodies, and screens, these forms transform political language into atmosphere. The circulation of Rām as a public image, however, did not emerge suddenly in the present moment. Throughout the twentieth century, the name moved across devotional practice, anti-colonial discourse, popular cinema, print culture, public ritual, and nationalist imagination- evolving, changing and reclaiming its visible and territorial presence in everyday life. Contains stickers, walls, paper, stairs, temple, flag, newspaper strips, tiles, poster, shrine, movie poster, plastic, stone, cloth.

title: Between Saguṇ and Nirguṇ (DHUN Gallery 3)
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: The Name appears differently, shifting between the formless (Nirguṇ) and the embodied (Saguṇ). The images trace the shifting visual life of the name across devotional, political, socio-cultural and mediated spaces. In some instances, Rām appears through saguṇ forms: embodied in idols, posters, calendar art, televised mythologies, or monumental iconography that give the divine a recognizable figure and presence. In others, the name moves through nirguṇ registers, where sound, script, repetition, color, or atmosphere become more important than figuration itself. Here, the divine is carried through chant, typography, rhythm, and circulation rather than through a fixed image. Contains stickers, posters, key chain, tiles, stones, clothes, paper malas, chains, prayer chains, dieties, shrines, metall grids, walls, prayer chains, wall paintings, grids, wristband, statues, flags, billboards, electronic meter, animal representation and pictures, wooden boards, plants, flower garlands, stone chains, amulets, hands, wires, stairs, electrical circuit, stone encarving.

title: Kabīr: The Name without Form (DHUN Gallery 5)
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: The figure and name of Rām have never belonged to a single form, theology, or tradition. In the bhakti movements of North India, poets such as Kabir reworked Rām beyond the boundaries of orthodox devotion, transforming the name into a critique of ritual hierarchy, caste, and religious division. This reconfiguration of Rām opened pathways for other devotional and poetic traditions. Across these traditions, the divine name circulated less as a singular image and more as a shared vocabulary of spiritual intimacy, social critique, and ethical life. The repetition of the name became a practice through which alternative religious communities imagined belonging outside dominant structures of authority. title: Digital Circulations and Shrines (DHUN Gallery 6)
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: In its digital emanation, the name circulates as pure repetition within networked space, detached from any single physical site yet constantly re-anchored through screens, platforms, and interfaces. It appears as text fragments, hashtags, thumbnails, reels, compressed images, and algorithmically amplified slogans, where visibility is governed less by permanence than by circulation, engagement, and replication.  Within these digital environments, the name becomes infrastructural rather than representational. It is embedded in the logics of sharing, forwarding, remixing, and reposting, where devotional utterance and political sign are indistinguishable from content flow. Each repetition is both identical and newly situated, generating a sense of presence that is continuous but dispersed across timelines and feeds. This mode of existence produces a form of presence without centrality: the name does not reside in a single image or authoritative form but persists as distributed signal across platforms. It is experienced through scrolling rather than viewing, through accumulation rather than encounter, and through algorithmic recurrence rather than fixed iconography.

title: Digital Circulations of Ram
description: This image was created specifically for the Dhun essay (2026) using generative AI tools (ChatGPT/OpenAI) in order to visually synthesize broader digital environments surrounding the contemporary circulation of Rām nām online. Rather than documenting a single real interface, application, or social media feed, the collage functions as a composite interpretive visualization bringing together recurring devotional, aesthetic, political, and technological motifs encountered during the research process. It is included as an analytical and illustrative image reflecting the multisensory and highly mediated circulation of sacred names within contemporary digital media ecologies. The image also forms part of a broader methodological reflection on AI assisted visual mediation within the project. Its compositional excesses, visual inconsistencies, and occasional inaccuracies, including distortions in text rendering and the blending of multiple visual registers, are not treated merely as technical flaws but as analytically revealing features of generative image systems themselves. The collage therefore also reflects how AI models interpret, aggregate, recombine, and reimagine religious imagery through patterns drawn from large scale digital training data, raising further questions about the remediation of religion, synthetic visual cultures, and the growing entanglement between devotional practice, digital infrastructures, and machine generated imaginaries.

title: Transition and Afterlife (DHUN Gallery 7)
creator: Piyush Kukrety; Borayin Larios; Kanika Pruthi
description: The chant moves collectively through the city, marking both death and transition as the living make way for the dead through streets already saturated with the name in countless other forms. Here, the utterance acquires an afterlife of its own, echoing across ritual movement, urban space, and public memory. The name accompanies the passage into the afterlife, moving alongside the dead as a final guide through transition. Repeated collectively in funeral processions and mourning rituals, the chant transforms grief into shared movement, carrying the departed through streets where the name already circulates in devotional, political, and everyday forms. In this moment, the utterance becomes more than prayer or proclamation; it functions as a companion between worlds, marking the threshold between presence and absence, life and death.
